The physics: why a mesoscale method exists¶

Your A2 code integrates the motion of individual molecular sites with a time step of about a femtosecond. Now consider what you would need to simulate a droplet of oil in water demixing, or a polymer solution flowing through a channel: micrometres of space and microseconds of time. That is roughly 1012 sites and 109 steps. Molecular dynamics cannot get there, and continuum fluid mechanics cannot resolve the individual polymer chains that matter. Dissipative particle dynamics (DPD) lives in that gap.

The trick is coarse-graining. One DPD bead is not an atom: it stands for a lump of fluid, a cluster of molecules moving together. Because a bead is a soft blob rather than a hard molecule, two beads may overlap, and the repulsion between them is soft:

𝐅ijC=aij(1−rijrc)𝐫^ijfor rij<rc,

finite even at rij=0. No r−12 wall means no violently fast collisions, which is what buys the very large time steps that make the method useful.

Coarse-graining throws away degrees of freedom, and they must come back as noise and friction. DPD adds two more pair forces:

𝐅ijD=−γωD(rij)(𝐫^ij·𝐯ij)𝐫^ij,𝐅ijR=σωR(rij)ζijΔt𝐫^ij.

The dissipative force damps the relative velocity of a pair, the random force kicks it. Neither is arbitrary: the fluctuation-dissipation theorem ties their amplitudes and their weight functions together (Eq. (5) of the paper, with ωD=[ωR]2 and σ2=2γkBT). Get that relation wrong and your system simply equilibrates to the wrong temperature, which is exactly what task B3 checks.

The decisive property is that all three forces act pairwise along the line between beads, so they conserve momentum. That is the difference between DPD and Brownian or Langevin dynamics, where the friction is with an implicit background that absorbs momentum. Conserved momentum means the correct long-wavelength behaviour emerges by itself: DPD reproduces hydrodynamics, so a DPD fluid flows, carries shear, and mediates hydrodynamic interactions between suspended objects. That is what makes it a mesoscale method rather than a fast approximation.

What does a bead stand for, quantitatively? Groot and Warren fix that by matching the compressibility of water at ρ=3, giving aii≈25kBT/rc for beads of the same type. Different types repel more strongly, aij>aii, and the excess drives demixing. The link to polymer physics is the Flory-Huggins parameter χ, which you will measure in task C3 and which turns out to depend linearly on Δa=aAB−aAA. Add springs between beads and you have polymer chains, whose demixing at much smaller Δa (the χN of Eq. (27)) is the subject of Part D.

What you will do, and the reference paper¶

You will convert your own MD code from Assignment 2 into a DPD code, verify it, and then use it to reproduce published results. There is no new starting code for A3, and so no \todo list to guide you: everything you have to build is stated in this notebook, in the section From your A2 code to a DPD code below and in the task texts. Read both before you change a line.

The reference is Groot and Warren, J. Chem. Phys. 107, 4423 (1997), handed out under Files ▸ Papers. Equation and figure numbers in this notebook refer to that paper. Reproducing a published result is the strongest form of validation available to you here: the numbers exist independently of your code, so agreement is evidence and disagreement is information.

Units: not the units of A2. In A2 the energy unit was kB×1 K, lengths were in Å and masses in amu, so kBT=293, the masses were about 15, the cut-off was 14 and the time step 0.001 (about 1 fs). DPD uses its own reduced units: the cut-off distance rc of the DPD interactions is the unit of length, the bead mass m the unit of mass, and the thermal energy kBT the unit of energy. The time unit follows as rcm/kBT. So rc=m=kBT=1, and every number in your A2 setparameters.c changes; the table in the next section lists them. Report everything in these units unless you say otherwise.

The integrator stays. Groot and Warren's Eq. (9) is a velocity-Verlet step in which the velocity-dependent forces of the new time step are evaluated with a predicted velocity 𝐯~=𝐯(t)+λΔt𝐟(t)/m. Your A2 loop already does this with λ=1/2: it calls calculate_forces after the first half kick and the position update, so the velocities the force routine sees are exactly 𝐯(t)+12Δt𝐟(t)/m. Keep the loop as it is. Use Δt=0.04 for all thermostatted runs, as the paper does.

Expect the conversion to be where the bugs are. Take small steps, run a short simulation after each change, and look at it in OVITO before you measure anything.

Part A: Implementing the DPD method¶

In the oral you should be able to: explain each of the three DPD pair forces and what it does to the system's energy and momentum; explain the 1/Δt in the random force; explain why σ and γ are not independent, and why the Berendsen thermostat had to go.

A1) DPD pair forces¶

Replace the Lennard-Jones interaction in calculate_forces_nb by the DPD pair forces of Eqs. (3), (4) and (8): the conservative force 𝐅C, the dissipative force 𝐅D, and the random force 𝐅R, with the weight functions of Eq. (6) and all three zero beyond rc. Use γ=4.5 and derive σ from the fluctuation-dissipation relation, Eq. (5). For the random force use ζij with mean zero and variance 1; uniformly distributed numbers from [−3,3] are recommended (see the discussion on p. 4426 of the paper). Make the conservative force type-dependent, aij per pair of types, stored the way A2 stored ϵij.

The potential energy your routine returns is that of the conservative force alone: the other two derive from no potential. Accumulate the virial from the conservative force only, as in the second line of Eq. (15).

Document in the cell below: the value of σ you derived and from which relation; how you ensured that ζij=ζji for a pair (what would break if it were not?); and where in your step the random force is drawn, given that it depends on Δt.

Implementation notes (A1): …

σ=2γkbT

ζij=ζji is ensured by implementing the gaussian only once per pair in the neighbour list and uses that same force for both particles.

The random force is drawn after the positions and boundary consitions are updated, but before the second half-step velocity update.

A2) Bead-spring chains¶

Adapt the code to chains of N beads: initialise_bond_connectivity must bond bead k to bead k+1 within each chain, and initialise_types must give all beads of a chain the same type, A or B. The spring force between bonded beads is

𝐟ij=−C𝐫ij,C=2kBTrc−2

(note the sign error in the paper's Eq. (25); the spring is always attractive). This is your A2 bond force with rest length zero.

Bonded pairs must also interact through the DPD pair forces. In A2 the excluded pairs would have overlapped the steep Lennard-Jones core, and the bonded terms already described their interaction. Neither holds here: the DPD repulsion is soft, and a chain bead is the same bead as a monomer, with the same repulsion from every neighbour. In the A2 code that means setting factor_12_nb, factor_13_nb and factor_14_nb to one, the opposite of A2: a factor zero excludes a pair, and a factor one treats it like any other pair (and skips the connectivity lookup altogether).

Write an initialisation for chain systems that avoids overstretched springs, for instance each chain as a random walk with steps of about the mean bond length. Give it an option to start all A chains in the half x<Lx/2 and all B chains in x>Lx/2, which every demixing run of Parts C and D uses.

Document your initialisation, and state what would go wrong physically if 1-2 and 1-3 pairs were excluded here, given that this is the opposite of what you did in A2.

Implementation notes (A2):

Initialisation (initialise_types, initialise_bond_connectivity, initialise_positions, initialise_velocities in code/initialise.c):

  • Types and bonds. Chain m is type A if m is even and type B if it is odd, so there are equal numbers of A and B chains and all beads of a chain have the same type. Bead k is bonded to bead k+1 within a chain (N−1 bonds per chain, none for N=1).
  • Chains as random walks. The first bead of a chain is put at a random position. Each next bead is placed at the fixed distance req=a/(a+C)=25/27=0.93 from the previous one, in a random direction (uniform on the sphere). This is the distance at which the spring force Cr balances the repulsion a(1−r), so the springs start almost unstretched, and it is close to the maximum of g(r) (C1).
  • Overlaps. A chain is redrawn if one of its beads comes closer than 0.5req to a bead that is already placed (at most 100 000 tries per chain). The repulsion is soft, so this only prevents beads from starting on top of each other.
  • Demixed start (demix_initialisation = 1). All beads of an A chain must lie in x<Lx/2 and all beads of a B chain in x>Lx/2, after periodic wrapping. This gives two flat interfaces perpendicular to x (every demixing run of C and D).
  • Velocities. Maxwell-Boltzmann with variance kBT/m per component, with the centre-of-mass velocity removed.
  • The structure is not equilibrated separately: the run itself does it, and the first part of each run is discarded in the analysis.

Demixed Initialization: (chain length = 5, not easily seen in OVITO)

Normal Initialization: (chain length = 5, not easily seen in OVITO)

What would go wrong if the 1-2 and 1-3 pairs were excluded. In A2 exclusion was right: the Lennard-Jones core is steep, and the bond and angle terms described how neighbours in a molecule interact. Here the springs have rest length 0 and are only attractive, and the only thing that keeps bonded beads apart is the soft DPD repulsion. Without it:

  • the chains would follow the springs alone, i.e. be ideal chains with ⟨R2⟩=3(N−1)kBT/C (6 for N=5) and too compact; with the repulsion, as we have it, D1 gives 6.75;
  • the dissipative and random forces between bonded neighbours would be missing, so their relative motion would not be thermostatted directly;
  • the chain beads would no longer behave like monomer beads. The mapping of χ onto Δa (Eq. 23) assumes that every pair of beads within rc interacts in the same way, whatever the connectivity.

A3) Radial distribution function¶

Implement on-the-fly calculation of the radial distribution function g(r), per type pair (AA, AB, BB), up to r=3. State your bin width and the normalisation you used, and how you convinced yourself the normalisation is right (a run whose answer you know in advance is the cheapest way; task B2 gives you one).

Implementation notes (A3):

The bin width used is 0.05, which gives 60 bins between r=0 and r=3. In each bin the code counts pairs which minimum-image distance falls between r=0 and r=3 and then compares the count with the expected number is they would be uniformly distributed in the box.

The g(r) function is then checked using the B2 run.

Part B: Verification for monomers (N = 1)¶

In the oral you should be able to: say which bug classes each of these three tests isolates, and why together they cover the code; derive the conservative pair potential; explain why the energy-conservation run needs a smaller timestep than a thermostatted run.

These three tests are designed to be run with parts of the physics switched off, which is what makes them sharp: each isolates one layer of the implementation. All three use the cubic box of side 10 with 3000 monomers and a=25 (see the run plan).

B1) Energy conservation¶

Derive the potential energy expression belonging to the conservative pair force. Disable the dissipative and random interactions and verify conservation of total energy.

Start these runs from an equilibrated state: the restart file written at the end of the thermostatted monomer-fluid run, as you used restart files in A2. Your initial positions are random, and their overlaps release so much potential energy that a run without the thermostat heats itself to well above kBT=1: still a test of energy conservation, but not of the state you simulate everywhere else.

Deliver:

  • the derivation of UC(r) from 𝐅C, and its value at r=0;
  • a figure of total, kinetic and potential energy against time for the conservative-only run;
  • a table of the relative energy drift for at least three time steps (Δt = 0.04, 0.02, 0.01, 0.005 are suggested), each run to the same physical time, with the observed scaling stated. Do not be alarmed if the largest time step does not conserve energy at all: say what you see, and explain why this run needs a smaller Δt than your thermostatted production runs do.

Results (B1):

  • What the conservative force alone represents. With the dissipative and random forces off, the beads interact only through the potential UC. That is an ordinary Hamiltonian system at constant N, V and total energy: K+U is conserved and any change is an integration error. When the other two forces are on they represent the coupling to the degrees of freedom that were coarse-grained away (a heat bath). They exchange energy with the beads, so the total energy then fluctuates around the value that belongs to kBT.
  • Runs. 3000 beads, a=25, started from the thermostatted monomer fluid at kBT=1 (end of the C1 run), t=8 for every Δt (code/run_b1.sh).
  • Result. In the figure (Δt=0.04) K and U exchange energy while the total stays flat. The maximum relative deviation from the initial energy is 1.1·10−3, 1.7·10−4, 5·10−5 and 8·10−6 for Δt = 0.04, 0.02, 0.01, 0.005, which scales as Δt2.3. Velocity Verlet is second order, and its error oscillates instead of drifting, so the endpoint value in the table is not a drift.
  • The largest step still conserves energy (0.1%): the force is bounded (≤a) and continuous, so the dynamics is smooth.
  • Why this run needs a smaller Δt than the production runs. With the thermostat on, the friction and noise absorb integration errors (they show up only as the small temperature error of B3). In this run nothing removes them, so they accumulate, and several Δt are needed to see how the error scales.

Derivation of Uc from Fc:

We use the relationship between the conservative force and potential energy:

FijC=−∇iU(rij)=−dUdrijr^ij

The conservative force: FijC=aij(1−rijrc)r^ij

thus: dUdrij=−aij(1−rijrc)

Which after integrating, gives:

UC(rij)=−aij(rij−rij22rc)+C

We know that at cut-off length (rij), UC = 0$, thus:

UC(rij)=0, which means:

0=−aij(rc−rc22rc)+C and:

C=12aijrc

And finally:

UC(rij)=12aijrc(1−rij2rc)2 for rij<rc

At rij=0, the potential goes to 12aijrc, the maximum.

from pathlib import Path
import re

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

DATA_DIR = Path("data")
PLOT_DT = 0.04  # Optionally set to 0.01, 0.02, 0.04, or 0.005.

# Filename suffix -> timestep. For example, B1_001.csv has dt = 0.01.
DT_BY_SUFFIX = {
    "001": 0.01,
    "002": 0.02,
    "004": 0.04,
    "0005": 0.005,
}

COLUMN_ALIASES = {
    "time": {"time", "t"},
    "step": {"step", "steps", "timestep", "iteration"},
    "kinetic": {"kinetic", "kineticenergy", "ekin", "ek", "k"},
    "potential": {"potential", "potentialenergy", "epot", "ep", "u"},
    "total": {"total", "totalenergy", "etot", "energy", "e"},
}

def normalise(name):
    return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]", "", str(name).lower())

def load_energy_file(path, dt):
    # Read CSV data with a header row.
    df = pd.read_csv(path, comment="#")
    df.columns = [str(column).strip() for column in df.columns]

    columns = {normalise(column): column for column in df.columns}

    def find_column(kind):
        return next(
            (columns[name] for name in COLUMN_ALIASES[kind] if name in columns),
            None,
        )

    time_col = find_column("time")
    step_col = find_column("step")
    kinetic_col = find_column("kinetic")
    potential_col = find_column("potential")
    total_col = find_column("total")

    if kinetic_col is None or potential_col is None:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{path.name}: couldn't identify kinetic and potential energy "
            f"columns. Found columns: {list(df.columns)}"
        )

    if step_col is not None:
        steps = pd.to_numeric(df[step_col], errors="coerce")
        time = steps * dt
    elif time_col is not None:
        time = pd.to_numeric(df[time_col], errors="coerce")
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"{path.name}: needs a time or step column.")

    kinetic = pd.to_numeric(df[kinetic_col], errors="coerce")
    potential = pd.to_numeric(df[potential_col], errors="coerce")

    if total_col is not None:
        total = pd.to_numeric(df[total_col], errors="coerce")
    else:
        total = kinetic + potential

    result = pd.DataFrame({
        "time": time,
        "kinetic": kinetic,
        "potential": potential,
        "total": total,
    }).dropna().sort_values("time")

    if result.empty:
        raise ValueError(f"{path.name}: no valid energy rows found.")

    return result

# Match B1_<suffix>.csv filenames and load only the specified B1 runs.
runs = {}
filename_pattern = re.compile(r"^B1_(\d+)\.csv$", re.IGNORECASE)

for path in sorted(DATA_DIR.glob("B1_*")):
    match = filename_pattern.match(path.name)
    if not match:
        continue

    suffix = match.group(1)
    if suffix not in DT_BY_SUFFIX:
        print(f"Skipping {path.name}: suffix {suffix!r} has no timestep mapping.")
        continue

    dt = DT_BY_SUFFIX[suffix]
    runs[dt] = (path, load_energy_file(path, dt))

if not runs:
    expected = ", ".join(f"B1_{suffix}.csv" for suffix in DT_BY_SUFFIX)
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"No matching B1 CSV files found in {DATA_DIR.resolve()}. "
        f"Expected: {expected}"
    )

# Restrict comparisons to the same physical time across all runs.
common_end_time = min(data["time"].max() for _, data in runs.values())
print(f"Comparing runs through t = {common_end_time:g}")

# Plot total, kinetic, and potential energy for the selected run.
plot_dt = PLOT_DT if PLOT_DT in runs else min(runs)
plot_path, plot_data = runs[plot_dt]
plot_data = plot_data[plot_data["time"] <= common_end_time]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
ax.plot(plot_data["time"], plot_data["total"], label="Total energy")
ax.plot(plot_data["time"], plot_data["kinetic"], label="Kinetic energy")
ax.plot(plot_data["time"], plot_data["potential"], label="Potential energy")
ax.set(
    xlabel="Time",
    ylabel="Energy",
    title=f"Conservative-only energy, dt = {plot_dt:g} ({plot_path.name})",
)
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Calculate endpoint drift and maximum deviation over the shared time interval.
rows = []

for dt, (path, data) in sorted(runs.items()):
    data = data[data["time"] <= common_end_time]
    time = data["time"].to_numpy()
    energy = data["total"].to_numpy()

    if len(time) < 2:
        print(f"Skipping drift calculation for {path.name}: too few samples.")
        continue

    initial_energy = energy[0]
    end_energy = np.interp(common_end_time, time, energy)
    energy_with_endpoint = np.append(energy, end_energy)

    if initial_energy == 0:
        endpoint_drift = np.nan
        max_deviation = np.nan
    else:
        endpoint_drift = 100 * (end_energy - initial_energy) / abs(initial_energy)
        max_deviation = (
            100 * np.max(np.abs(energy_with_endpoint - initial_energy))
            / abs(initial_energy)
        )

    rows.append({
        "dt": dt,
        "file": path.name,
        "comparison end time": common_end_time,
        "relative endpoint drift (%)": endpoint_drift,
        "maximum relative deviation (%)": max_deviation,
    })

drift_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("dt")
display(drift_table)

# Estimate the power-law scaling from the maximum deviation (the endpoint value of an oscillating error
# is not a drift, so it is not used for the scaling)
valid = drift_table[drift_table["maximum relative deviation (%)"] > 0]
if len(valid) >= 2:
    slope = np.polyfit(np.log(valid["dt"]), np.log(valid["maximum relative deviation (%)"]), 1)[0]
    print(f"Approximate observed scaling: maximum relative deviation ~ dt^{slope:.2f}")
else:
    print("Not enough nonzero deviations to estimate timestep scaling.")

B2) Ideal-gas structure¶

Disable the conservative interactions, keeping the dissipative and random forces on. The beads then interact only through friction and noise, so their equilibrium structure must be that of an ideal gas.

Deliver a figure of g(r) for this run, showing it is flat and equal to 1 within the noise, and a sentence on what a non-flat result would have told you (this test catches both a broken g(r) normalisation and a conservative force that is not really off).

B3) Velocity statistics¶

Verify that the velocity distribution matches the imposed temperature (Maxwellian, with the correct variance), independent of the conservative interactions.

Deliver:

  • a figure of the velocity histogram with the Maxwell-Boltzmann prediction on top, for a run with the conservative force on and one with it off;
  • a table of the measured kBT from the variance in both cases, next to the imposed value, and a sentence comparing the deviation you find with what Groot and Warren report for the Verlet scheme with λ=1/2 at Δt=0.04 (Fig. 1 and the text beside it);
  • a short statement of what this verifies about your σ and γ: if you had used a wrong fluctuation-dissipation relation, what would this table look like?

Conclusion B2

  • Result. g(r) is 1 for AA, AB and BB: the bin values have mean 1.00 and standard deviation 0.01 to 0.02. Only the first bins (r<0.15) are higher, because there are very few pairs there (0.6 expected per sample in the first bin) and the noise is large.
  • Why this is the configuration of an ideal gas. With the conservative force off, the remaining forces are not derived from a potential, so U=0. They only change velocities, and by the fluctuation-dissipation relation they leave the equilibrium distribution unchanged. The equilibrium positions then have Boltzmann weight e−U/kBT=1: all positions are equally likely and independent of each other. That is the ideal gas, with g(r)=1.
  • What a non-flat result would have told us. Either the g(r) normalisation is wrong (this happened several times in our first tests), or the conservative force is not really off (a peak near r=0.9 and a depletion at small r, as in C1).

B3 conclusion:

  • What was measured. Velocity components of all beads, sampled every 100 steps after the first 4000 (241 500 samples per type and component), for a run with the conservative force on and one with it off (a=25, box 103, Δt=0.04). The histograms follow the Maxwell-Boltzmann Gaussian of variance kBT/m closely (figure) and the mean velocities are zero within 0.005.
  • Table. The measured kBT is 1.03 for every type and component (spread ±0.005): 3.0% above the imposed value with the conservative force on and 3.1% with it off. The temperature does not depend on the conservative force, as it must: it is fixed by the dissipative and random forces.
  • Comparison with Groot and Warren. For the Verlet scheme with λ=12 at Δt=0.04 they find a temperature 2% too high (3% at Δt=0.05; Fig. 1 and the text beside it, at ρ=4 and σ=3). We find 3%: the same order and sign. This is a time-step error of the integrator, not an error in the forces. We did not check that it shrinks with Δt.
  • What this verifies about σ and γ. The random force heats and the friction cools, and they balance at kBT=σ2/2γ. With σ2=2γkBT this is the imposed temperature. If σ2 were wrong by a factor f, the table would show a temperature off by that factor (for example 2 instead of 1 for f=2), not 3%. The shape of the histogram would still be Gaussian, so the variance is what tests the relation.

Part C: Validation for monomers (N = 1)¶

In the oral you should be able to: say what agreement with a published simulation result does and does not validate; explain how χ is measured from composition profiles and what must be true of the profiles first; explain the sign, magnitude and factor of two of your surface tension.

Every demixing run (C2, C3, C4, and Part D) uses the same geometry. The box is 20×10×10, elongated along x, with 6000 beads, and starts with A in the half x<10 and B in the half x>10. The two phases then form two flat slabs with two flat interfaces perpendicular to x, and the two bulk regions are wide enough to read a composition from. In a cubic box the system can separate along any axis, or not into flat slabs at all, and then neither the composition profile nor the surface tension means anything. Groot and Warren elongate their box along z; we use x throughout, so read their z as our x.

The composition profile is the number density of A and of B in thin slabs perpendicular to x (a bin width of about 0.2 to 0.5), averaged over the run after equilibration, and the A fraction ϕA(x)=ρA/(ρA+ρB) computed from them. Write it out in blocks during the run (every few thousand steps), not only once at the end: C2 asks when the profile became steady, and the error estimates of C3 come from the scatter between blocks.

C1) Radial distribution function¶

Reproduce the g(r) of Fig. 2 (ρ=3, a=25).

Deliver a figure with your g(r) and the published curve on the same axes (digitise a few points from the figure if you have no data file), and a sentence on where they agree and where they do not. State your run length and how you know g(r) has converged.

Results (C1):

  • Run. 3000 beads, a=25, ρ=3, 20 000 steps; g(r) sampled every 20 steps after step 4000 (bin width 0.05).
  • Agreement with Fig. 2. g=0 at small r (the soft core can overlap, but only at a cost), one maximum of 1.15 at r≈0.9, and g→1 beyond rc. The curve also dips to about 0.95 near r≈1.2 (outside the range of the paper's figure).
  • Difference. Between r=0.5 and 0.75 our curve lies about 0.1 above the points we read off the figure. We read these points by eye (accuracy 0.05 to 0.1), so the difference is not significant. A real difference would mean that the repulsion acts over a different range; the published data would be needed to decide.
  • Converged. The four blocks of 4000 steps agree within 0.005 at the peak (zoom panel).
  • What this validates. The conservative force, the cut-off and the g(r) normalisation in a fluid with all forces on. It says nothing about unlike pairs.

C2) Binary demixing¶

Reproduce the phase separation of Fig. 6, using the parameters in its caption (aAB=37) and the geometry above.

Deliver:

  • a snapshot of the demixed system (OVITO, beads coloured by type);
  • a figure of the composition profile along x, showing the two bulk plateaus and the two interfaces;
  • a statement of how long the run needed to reach a steady profile, and how you decided it had.

Results (C2):

  • Run. 20×10×10 box, 6000 beads, aAB=37, A started in x<10 and B in x>10, 60 000 steps.
  • Snapshot (OVITO). Two flat slabs, A (red) and B (blue), separated by two flat interfaces perpendicular to x (the second one lies across the periodic boundary, at x=0≡20).
  • Profile. Two plateaus of almost pure A and pure B, and two interfaces about 2rc wide. The total density is about 3 in the bulk with a small dip at the interfaces, as in Fig. 6.
  • When it was steady, and how we decided. The bulk ϕA of the B-rich phase is the slowest quantity to settle: the initial interface is sharp, and A beads still have to diffuse into the B phase. We therefore follow it block by block (bottom panel). The blocks ending at steps 5000, 10 000 and 15 000 are 0.03, 0.04 and 0.055, still changing. After step 20 000 the blocks scatter by 0.003 around 0.041 without a trend (a straight-line fit gives −0.0007±0.0010 per 10 000 steps, zero within error). So the profile is steady from about step 20 000 (t=800), and the first 20 000 steps are discarded in all averages.

# C2: OVITO snapshot, composition profile, steady state

USE_FROM = 20000                                   # first 20 000 steps are discarded

avg = prof[prof.step_end > USE_FROM].groupby("x")[["rho_A", "rho_B"]].mean()

(k, _), cov = np.polyfit(steady.index, steady.values, 1, cov=True)

C3) Measuring the χ-parameter¶

Measure χ with Eq. (18) from the composition profiles of demixed runs at ρ=3, for this edition's series

aAB∈{35, 39, 43, 47},aAA=aBB=25.

For monomers NA=1, and ϕA in Eq. (18) is the A fraction in the bulk of the B-rich phase. Read it from the plateau of the profile, away from both interfaces.

Deliver:

  • a figure with the four composition profiles;
  • a table of the bulk compositions and the resulting χ per aAB, each with an error estimate;
  • a figure of χ against Δa=aAB−aAA with a linear fit, the fitted slope stated, and the slope of Eq. (24) (Fig. 7) for comparison. Groot and Warren fit only the points with χ>3 (p. 4429), with the same integrator and Δt as yours: compare like with like, and report the fit over all four points as well.

Then state what must be true of the profiles before Eq. (18) may be applied at all, and confirm that it is true of yours.

Results (C3):

  • Method. ϕA is the A fraction in the B-rich bulk (12.5<x<17.5; time average after step 20 000; error: standard error over 7 blocks). Eq. (18) for N=1 gives χ=ln[(1−ϕA)/ϕA]/(1−2ϕA). It follows from equal chemical potential of A in both phases; for this symmetric system the A-rich phase has the A fraction 1−ϕA.
  • Slope of χ against Δa. Eq. (24): 0.286, from a line through the origin. Our points with χ>3 (aAB = 39, 43, 47) give 0.268 with a free intercept and 0.288 through the origin. All four points give 0.308 and 0.286. The through-origin slopes are the like-for-like comparison and agree with Eq. (24). The point aAB=35 has χ=2.7<3, close to the critical point where Eq. (18) is not reliable, so it is excluded from the χ>3 fit.
  • What must be true before Eq. (18) can be used, and our check (columns of the table):
    1. Two coexisting bulk phases in a steady state. The bulk ϕA shows no trend over the blocks used (trend_in_errors: −0.2, −0.8, +0.1, −2.1 standard errors; the last is marginal for a very small ϕA).
    2. A flat plateau, away from the interfaces. The slope of ϕA(x) in the window is at most 0.0015 per rc (plateau_slope), and the window is at least 2.5rc from both interfaces.
    3. Symmetric coexistence. The A-rich bulk has the B fraction ϕA of the B-rich bulk (mirror_check ≤0.0024). We did not test that the result is independent of the starting configuration (one start per run).
In [6]:
# C3: composition profiles; chi against Delta a with linear fit
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RUNS = {35: "C3_a35", 39: "C3_a39", 43: "C3_a43", 47: "C3_a47"}
EQ24_SLOPE = 0.286            # Groot & Warren, Eq. (24), rho = 3
USE_FROM = 20000

def chi_of_phi(phi):          # Eq. (18) with N_A = N_B = 1
    return np.log((1 - phi) / phi) / (1 - 2 * phi)

rows, profiles = [], {}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
for aab, run in RUNS.items():
    p = pd.read_csv(f"data/{run}_profile.csv")
    p["phi"] = p.rho_A / (p.rho_A + p.rho_B)
    q = p[p.step_end > USE_FROM]
    avg = q.groupby("x").phi.mean()
    ax.plot(avg.index, avg.values, label=f"$a_{{AB}}={aab}$")
    win = q[(q.x > 12.5) & (q.x < 17.5)]
    per_block = win.groupby("block").phi.mean()                  # bulk of the B-rich phase
    phi, dphi = per_block.mean(), per_block.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(per_block))
    chi = chi_of_phi(phi)
    dchi = abs(chi_of_phi(phi + dphi) - chi_of_phi(phi - dphi)) / 2
    # flatness of the plateau: slope of phi(x) in the window
    slope = np.polyfit(win.groupby("x").phi.mean().index, win.groupby("x").phi.mean().values, 1)[0]
    # steady state: trend of the bulk phi_A over the blocks used, in units of its error
    (kt, _), cov = np.polyfit(per_block.index, per_block.values, 1, cov=True)
    # symmetric coexistence: the A-rich bulk must contain a B fraction equal to phi_A of the B-rich bulk
    arich = q[(q.x > 2.5) & (q.x < 7.5)].groupby("block").phi.mean().mean()
    rows.append(dict(a_AB=aab, delta_a=aab - 25, phi_A=phi, err_phi=dphi, chi=chi, err_chi=dchi,
                     plateau_slope=slope, trend_in_errors=kt / np.sqrt(cov[0, 0]), mirror_check=arich + phi - 1))
ax.set(xlabel="x", ylabel="$\\phi_A(x)$", yscale="log", title="C3: composition profiles")
ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

tab = pd.DataFrame(rows)
display(tab.round(4))

da, chi, err = tab.delta_a.values, tab.chi.values, tab.err_chi.values
def fit(mask):
    w = 1 / np.maximum(err[mask], 1e-9)
    k, b = np.polyfit(da[mask], chi[mask], 1, w=w)
    k0 = np.sum(da[mask] * chi[mask]) / np.sum(da[mask] ** 2)       # through the origin
    return k, b, k0
sel = chi > 3
k_all, b_all, k0_all = fit(np.ones_like(sel))
k_hi, b_hi, k0_hi = fit(sel)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.5))
ax.errorbar(da, chi, err, fmt="o", capsize=3, label="measured")
xs = np.linspace(0, 24, 50)
ax.plot(xs, k_all * xs + b_all, label=f"fit, all 4 points: slope {k_all:.3f}")
ax.plot(xs, k_hi * xs + b_hi, "--", label=f"fit, $\\chi>3$ ({sel.sum()} points): slope {k_hi:.3f}")
ax.plot(xs, EQ24_SLOPE * xs, "k:", label="Eq. (24): $0.286\\,\\Delta a$")

print(f"slope, chi > 3 ({sel.sum()} pts) : {k_hi:.3f}  (through origin {k0_hi:.3f})")

C4) Surface tension (new this edition)¶

For the same demixed runs as C3, obtain the interfacial tension from Eq. (31). With the interface normal along x it reads

σs=∫[pxx(x)−12(pyy(x)+pzz(x))]dx,

the normal minus the tangential pressure, integrated across the interface. You do not need the pressure as a function of x. What you need is this:

  1. The diagonal of the pressure tensor of the whole box, at every sampling step: Pαα=1V[∑imviα2+∑i<jrij,αFij,α], α=x,y,z, with 𝐅ij the conservative and spring forces, as in Eq. (15). Your A2 code accumulates only the scalar virial ∑𝐫ij·𝐅ij; accumulate its three components separately, in the same place.
  2. The step from Eq. (31) to those three numbers. Take the integral over the whole periodic box. Derive σs in terms of Lx and the box averages Pxx, Pyy, Pzz, say where the two interfaces in the box enter, and explain why the bulk regions add nothing to the integral.
  3. A time average with an honest error. Successive samples are strongly correlated, so the naive standard error of the mean is too small; use block averages.
  4. A control run at aAB=25, with the same separated start: one phase, no interface, so σs must vanish within its error. That checks your tensor for a bias between x and the other two directions; a wrong overall factor would pass it, so check the magnitude too, against Groot and Warren's monomer surface tension, Eq. (36).

Deliver:

  • a table and a figure of σs against Δa, with error bars, including the control;
  • your derivation of item 2;
  • a discussion of three things: the sign of σs and why it must be that sign for a stable interface; the trend with Δa; and the limit as Δa approaches the mixing point, where the two phases become identical.

Results (C4):

Derivation. Integrate Eq. (31) over the whole periodic box, 0<x<Lx. Because ∫pαα(x)dx=LxPαα (the box-averaged pressure that we sample), the integral is Lx[Pxx−12(Pyy+Pzz)]. The box contains two interfaces (at x≈Lx/2 and at x≈0≡Lx) and Eq. (31) is for one, so

σs=Lx2[Pxx−12(Pyy+Pzz)].

In the bulk the fluid is isotropic (pxx=pyy=pzz), so the bulk adds nothing and only the interfaces contribute.

Method. Pαα=1V[∑mvα2+∑rαFα] with the conservative force (Eq. 15), sampled every 10 steps, first 20% discarded. The error is the standard error of 8 block means. Successive samples are 0.4 time units apart and practically uncorrelated here (lag-1 autocorrelation ≤0.03, column lag1_autocorr), so the naive error (0.015) and the block error (0.011 to 0.025) agree within the scatter expected from only 8 blocks. We quote the block error.

Results (table and figure above):

  • Control (aAB=25): σs=0.009±0.017, zero within error, with P=23.7 as the equation of state predicts. There is no bias between x and y,z.
  • Magnitude. Measured/Eq. (36) is 0.99 to 1.02 for Δa≥14 and 1.05 to 1.08 for Δa=10,12, so the overall factor (including the factor 2) is right and not only the zero of the control.
  • Sign. σs>0: the interface costs free energy. With a negative value the interface would grow until the phases mix, so two stable slabs would not exist. In terms of pressure, the tangential pressure at the interface is lower than the normal one.
  • Trend. σs grows with Δa (0.23 to 1.79 for Δa=10 to 22): the more unlike beads repel, the more the interface costs.
  • Limit. σs→0 at the mixing point, where the two phases become identical and there is no interface. Eq. (36) goes to zero at χ=2.36 as (1−2.36/χ)3/2.

# C4: sigma_s against Delta a, with the control
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RUNS = {0: "C4_a25", 10: "C3_a35", 12: "C2_a37", 14: "C3_a39", 18: "C3_a43", 22: "C3_a47"}
LX, NBLOCK, SKIP = 20.0, 8, 0.2
def EQ36(delta_a, rho=3.0):
    """Groot-Warren Eq. (36): sigma = 0.75 rho kT r_c chi^0.26 [1 - 2.36/chi]^1.5, with chi = 0.286 Delta a (rho = 3)."""
    chi = 0.286 * delta_a
    return 0.75 * rho * chi ** 0.26 * (1 - 2.36 / chi) ** 1.5

rows = []
for da, run in RUNS.items():
    p = pd.read_csv(f"data/{run}_pressure.csv")
    p = p.iloc[int(SKIP * len(p)):]
    s = 0.5 * LX * (p.Pxx - 0.5 * (p.Pyy + p.Pzz))               # instantaneous sigma_s
    blocks = np.array_split(s.values, NBLOCK)
    bm = np.array([b.mean() for b in blocks])
    naive = s.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(s))
    lag1 = np.corrcoef(s.values[:-1], s.values[1:])[0, 1]          # correlation of successive samples (0.4 time units apart)
    rows.append(dict(delta_a=da, a_AB=25 + da, sigma_s=bm.mean(), err_blocks=bm.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(NBLOCK),
                     err_naive=naive, lag1_autocorr=lag1, P_iso=(p.Pxx + p.Pyy + p.Pzz).mean() / 3))
tab = pd.DataFrame(rows)
display(tab.round(4))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.5))
ax.errorbar(tab.delta_a, tab.sigma_s, tab.err_blocks, fmt="o-", capsize=3, label="this work (block error)")

ctrl = tab[tab.delta_a == 0].iloc[0]
print(f"control: sigma_s = {ctrl.sigma_s:.4f} +- {ctrl.err_blocks:.4f}  (zero within {abs(ctrl.sigma_s)/ctrl.err_blocks:.1f} sigma)")

Part D: Validation for chains (N > 1)¶

In the oral you should be able to: explain why longer chains demix at smaller Δa, and what Eq. (27)'s χN means for a symmetric blend.

For chains of equal length NA=NB=N, Eq. (18) gives the product χN, with ϕA the fraction of A beads in the B-rich phase. Demixing is governed by χN, so the values of Δa that work for monomers are far too large for chains: at Δa=16 every chain length used here demixes completely, no A bead is left in the B-rich phase, ϕA=0 and Eq. (18) cannot be evaluated. That is why Part D uses much smaller Δa, and different values for each N (see the run plan). Close to its critical point every interface is wide, and a chain is several bead diameters long: check, for each run, that the part of the profile you call bulk is really flat.

D1) Snapshot¶

Provide a snapshot of equilibrated bead-spring chains with N=5 (a=25 for every pair, cubic box), and a number characterising the chains themselves: the mean-square end-to-end distance, compared with that of an ideal chain with the same springs (derive it: N−1 independent harmonic bonds with spring constant C). This is your check that the springs and the initialisation are doing what you think; say why the two numbers need not agree.

D2) Two-phase simulations¶

Perform demixing simulations for chain lengths N=3, 5 and 10, all at Δa=3 (aAB=28).

Deliver a figure with the composition profiles of the three chain lengths on one set of axes, in the style of Fig. 6, so the effect of N is visible in one figure, and a snapshot of each.

D3) χ-parameter for chains¶

Measure χ for the chain systems, with a separate series of Δa for each chain length:

N Δa
3 3, 5, 7
5 2, 3.5, 5
10 1, 1.5, 2

(N=3 at Δa=3 is the D2 run.)

Deliver a table of χ and χN against N and Δa, and a figure comparing your χN/Δa with Eq. (27) and Fig. 8. Then answer the physical question: at fixed Δa, why do longer chains demix more readily? Argue it from your table, from χN rather than from the pictures.

Results (D1-D3): D1 and D2 are answered below their cells. D3:

  • Method. As in C3, for 9 runs (N = 3, 5, 10; 60 000 steps): ϕA is the fraction of A beads in the B-rich bulk and χN=ln[(1−ϕA)/ϕA]/(1−2ϕA) (Eq. 18).
  • Result. χN/Δa is 0.84 to 0.97 for N=3, 1.42 to 1.48 for N=5 and 2.3 to 2.8 for N=10, against 0.92, 1.53 and 3.06 from Eq. (27) (0.306N). It grows about linearly with N (figure). A fit through the origin gives 0.27 against 0.306.
  • Reliability. N=3 and 5 agree with Eq. (27) within 5 to 8%. The N=10 runs are less reliable: at Δa=1 the B-rich phase was still taking up A chains at the end of the run (not equilibrated), and at Δa=1.5 and 2 only a few chains are in the bulk window, so the values are noisy. Points with χN<3 (for N=3, Δa=3; N=5, Δa=2; N=10, Δa=1) lie close to the critical value, where Eq. (18) is not reliable.
  • Why longer chains demix more readily. χ per bead depends on Δa only (χ/Δa is 0.23 to 0.32 for every N). But a chain of N beads pays the contact penalty for each of its beads, while the gain in mixing entropy is only about kBT per chain. So χN=0.306NΔa grows with N: at Δa=5, χN is 4.4 for N=3 and 7.1 for N=5; at Δa=2 it is 3.0 for N=5 and 4.7 for N=10. The critical value χN=2 is reached at Δa≈6.5/N.

# Results D2
from pathlib import Path
import csv

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


DATA_DIR = Path("data")
CHAIN_LENGTHS = (3, 5, 10)
PDB_FILES = {n: DATA_DIR / f"D2_N{n}.pdb" for n in CHAIN_LENGTHS}

BOX = np.array([20.0, 10.0, 10.0])
BIN_WIDTH = 0.25
EQUILIBRATION_FRACTION = 0.33
EXPECTED_BEADS_PER_FRAME = 6000


def read_composition_profile(pdb_path):
    """Return time-averaged bead densities and A fraction versus x."""
    n_bins = round(BOX[0] / BIN_WIDTH)
    edges = np.linspace(0.0, BOX[0], n_bins + 1)
    frames_a = []
    frames_b = []
    counts_a = np.zeros(n_bins, dtype=np.int64)
    counts_b = np.zeros(n_bins, dtype=np.int64)
    in_model = False
    beads_in_model = 0

    with pdb_path.open(encoding="utf-8") as pdb:
        for line in pdb:
            record = line[:6].strip()

            if record == "MODEL":
                in_model = True
                counts_a.fill(0)
                counts_b.fill(0)
                beads_in_model = 0

            elif record == "ENDMDL" and in_model:
                if beads_in_model != EXPECTED_BEADS_PER_FRAME:
                    raise ValueError(
                        f"{pdb_path}: expected {EXPECTED_BEADS_PER_FRAME} beads "
                        f"in a frame, got {beads_in_model}"
                    )
                frames_a.append(counts_a.copy())
                frames_b.append(counts_b.copy())
                in_model = False

            elif record == "HETATM" and in_model:
                bead_type = line[12:16].strip()
                x = float(line[30:38]) % BOX[0]
                bin_index = min(int(x / BIN_WIDTH), n_bins - 1)

                if bead_type == "A":
                    counts_a[bin_index] += 1
                elif bead_type == "B":
                    counts_b[bin_index] += 1
                else:
                    raise ValueError(
                        f"{pdb_path}: unexpected bead type {bead_type!r}"
                    )

                beads_in_model += 1

    if in_model:
        raise ValueError(f"{pdb_path}: final PDB model is missing ENDMDL")
    if not frames_a:
        raise ValueError(f"{pdb_path}: no PDB trajectory frames found")

    first_equilibrated_frame = int(len(frames_a) * EQUILIBRATION_FRACTION)
    if first_equilibrated_frame >= len(frames_a):
        raise ValueError(f"{pdb_path}: no frames remain after equilibration skip")

    used_a = np.asarray(frames_a[first_equilibrated_frame:])
    used_b = np.asarray(frames_b[first_equilibrated_frame:])

    slab_volume = BIN_WIDTH * BOX[1] * BOX[2]
    rho_a = used_a.mean(axis=0) / slab_volume
    rho_b = used_b.mean(axis=0) / slab_volume
    rho_total = rho_a + rho_b

    phi_a = np.divide(
        rho_a,
        rho_total,
        out=np.full_like(rho_a, np.nan),
        where=rho_total > 0,
    )
    x_centers = 0.5 * (edges[:-1] + edges[1:])

    return x_centers, rho_a, rho_b, phi_a, len(used_a)


profiles = {}

for n, pdb_path in PDB_FILES.items():
    if pdb_path.is_file():
        profiles[n] = read_composition_profile(pdb_path)
    else:
        # The trajectory files are not handed in: use the profiles saved by an earlier run of this cell.
        saved = np.genfromtxt(DATA_DIR / f"D2_N{n}_composition.csv", delimiter=",", names=True)
        profiles[n] = (saved["x"], saved["rho_A"], saved["rho_B"], saved["phi_A"], None)


# The D2 requirement is one composition-profile figure with all three N values.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

for n, (x, rho_a, rho_b, phi_a, frames_used) in profiles.items():
    ax.plot(
        x,
        phi_a,
        marker="o",
        markersize=2.5,
        linewidth=1.4,
        label=f"N={n}" + (f" ({frames_used} equilibrated frames)" if frames_used else ""),
    )

ax.set(
    xlabel="x",
    ylabel=r"A-bead fraction $\phi_A(x)$",
    xlim=(0, BOX[0]),
    ylim=(0, 1),
    title="D2 composition profiles",
)
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()

figure_path = Path("data/D2_composition_profiles.png")
fig.savefig(figure_path, dpi=200)
plt.show()


# Save the numerical profiles as CSVs as well.
for n, (x, rho_a, rho_b, phi_a, _) in profiles.items():
    if not PDB_FILES[n].is_file():
        continue
    output_path = DATA_DIR / f"D2_N{n}_composition.csv"

    with output_path.open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as output_file:
        writer = csv.writer(output_file)
        writer.writerow(["x", "rho_A", "rho_B", "phi_A"])
        writer.writerows(zip(x, rho_a, rho_b, phi_a))

# D3: chi N for chains from the composition profiles, against Eq. (27)
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

RUNS = [(3, 3), (3, 5), (3, 7), (5, 2), (5, 3.5), (5, 5), (10, 1), (10, 1.5), (10, 2)]   # (N, Delta a)
USE_FROM = 20000                  # discard the first 20 000 steps, as in C2/C3
WINDOW = (12.5, 17.5)             # bulk of the B-rich phase, away from both interfaces (at x = 10 and 20)
EQ27 = 0.306                      # Groot-Warren Eq. (27): chi N / Delta a = 0.306 N

def chiN_of_phi(phi):             # Eq. (18) with N_A = N_B = N: chi N = ln[(1-phi)/phi] / (1-2 phi)
    return np.log((1 - phi) / phi) / (1 - 2 * phi)

def run_name(N, da):
    return f"D3_N{N}_da{da:g}"

rows, profiles = [], {}
for N, da in RUNS:
    p = pd.read_csv(f"data/{run_name(N, da)}_profile.csv")
    p["phi"] = p.rho_A / (p.rho_A + p.rho_B)          # A-bead fraction: the beads of A chains count as A
    q = p[p.step_end > USE_FROM]
    profiles[(N, da)] = q.groupby("x").phi.mean()
    win = q[(q.x > WINDOW[0]) & (q.x < WINDOW[1])]
    per_block = win.groupby("block").phi.mean()
    phi, dphi = per_block.mean(), per_block.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(per_block))
    chiN = chiN_of_phi(phi)
    dchiN = abs(chiN_of_phi(phi + dphi) - chiN_of_phi(phi - dphi)) / 2
    prof = win.groupby("x").phi.mean()
    slope = np.polyfit(prof.index, prof.values, 1)[0]        # flatness of the plateau, d(phi)/dx
    # the A-rich bulk (x = 2.5..7.5) must give the mirror image 1 - phi
    arich = q[(q.x > 2.5) & (q.x < 7.5)].groupby("block").phi.mean().mean()
    rows.append(dict(N=N, delta_a=da, phi_A=phi, err_phi=dphi, chi_N=chiN, err_chi_N=dchiN,
                     chi=chiN / N, chi_N_over_da=chiN / da, plateau_slope=slope,
                     mirror_check=arich + phi - 1, blocks=len(per_block)))
tab = pd.DataFrame(rows)
pd.set_option("display.width", 200)
display(tab.round(4))

# --- figure 1: the profiles, one panel per chain length
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.8), sharey=True)
for ax, N in zip(axes, (3, 5, 10)):
    for (n, da), prof in profiles.items():
        if n == N:
            ax.plot(prof.index, prof.values, label=f"$\\Delta a={da:g}$")
    ax.set(xlabel="x", title=f"$N={N}$", yscale="log")
    ax.axvspan(*WINDOW, color="gray", alpha=0.15)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.legend()
axes[0].set_ylabel("$\\phi_A(x)$ (A beads)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# --- figure 2: chi N / Delta a against N, with Eq. (27); N = 1 from the monomer runs of C3
mono = []
for a_ab in (39, 43, 47):                                  # the C3 runs with chi > 3
    p = pd.read_csv(f"data/C3_a{a_ab}_profile.csv"); p["phi"] = p.rho_A / (p.rho_A + p.rho_B)
    q = p[(p.step_end > USE_FROM) & (p.x > WINDOW[0]) & (p.x < WINDOW[1])]
    mono.append(chiN_of_phi(q.groupby("block").phi.mean().mean()) / (a_ab - 25))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.5))
ax.errorbar(tab.N, tab.chi_N_over_da, tab.err_chi_N / tab.delta_a, fmt="o", capsize=3, label="this work, chains")
for (N, da), y in zip(zip(tab.N, tab.delta_a), tab.chi_N_over_da):
    ax.annotate(f"{da:g}", (N, y), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(5, -9), fontsize=8)
ax.plot([1], [np.mean(mono)], "s", color="gray", label="$N=1$ (C3, $\\chi>3$)")
ns = np.linspace(0, 11, 20)
ax.plot(ns, EQ27 * ns, "k--", label="Eq. (27): $0.306\\,N$")
ax.set(xlabel="N", ylabel="$\\chi N/\\Delta a$", title="D3: $\\chi N/\\Delta a$ against chain length (labels: $\\Delta a$)")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# slope of chi N / Delta a against N: through the origin, for all points and for the points with chi N > 3
for label, sel in (("all 9 points", tab.chi_N > 0), ("points with chi N > 3", tab.chi_N > 3)):
    t = tab[sel]
    k0 = np.sum(t.N * t.chi_N_over_da) / np.sum(t.N ** 2)
    print(f"slope of chi N / Delta a against N through the origin, {label} ({len(t)}): {k0:.3f}   (Eq. 27: {EQ27})")
print(f"N = 1, mean of chi / Delta a for the three C3 runs with chi > 3: {np.mean(mono):.3f}")

Lessons learned¶

What would you do differently if you started over? What surprised you? What broke first in the conversion from MD to DPD, and how did you find it? (Standing questions in the oral, so write the honest version.)

Lessons learned:

  • What broke first. The g(r) normalisation: the first versions were not flat for the ideal gas (B2), which is why B2 exists. The next failure was in B1: our first energy-conservation data wandered by about 1% independent of Δt, which is the signature of a noise force that was still on, not of integration error. The Δt scaling exposed it, and we regenerated the data with a script (code/run_b1.sh). Smaller slips were in the notebook: the B2 plot read an energy log with a similar file name instead of the g(r) file.
  • What surprised us. How well the results agree with the paper: χ/Δa=0.29 and the surface tension within 1% of Eq. (36) at large Δa. The control run alone (it only checks the zero) would not have confirmed the factor of two in σs. The g(r) blocks are so close that their scatter is invisible on a normal plot.
  • What we would do differently. (1) Write the analysis (profiles, pressure tensor, block output) once and use it for every run, instead of two composition-profile writers. (2) Keep every run as a script from the start, so that the build and run log is the script. (3) Keep the data that the notebook reads in data/ from the beginning (the D2 cell reads trajectory files that are not handed in). (4) Digitise the published curves early. (5) Check that a cell reads the file it names.

Hand-in¶

One zip per group, layout exactly:

<group>_A3.zip
├── A3.ipynb     this notebook, filled in and executed
│                (all outputs present; task cells untouched)
├── A3.html      python3 nb2html.py A3.ipynb
├── code/        all .c/.h + README.md; must build with
│                gcc -O3 *.c -o dpd -lm    (no binaries)
└── data/        every data file this notebook loads

Long runs are done in the terminal; record the exact commands in the Build & run log and let the notebook load the saved output from data/. Handed in executed, the notebook must open and display without rerunning anything.

Before you submit, check your own zip:

python3 check_my_submission.py <group>_A3.zip --release A3.ipynb

where --release is a freshly downloaded, unmodified A3.ipynb. It verifies the layout, that the task cells are untouched, that every cell has been executed, that your C code compiles, and that every path and link in the notebook is relative and present in the zip. Fix what it reports, then submit. Setting up the Python environment (requirements.txt, both helper scripts) is described on the Canvas page Working on the assignments.
